content:
Osteoporosis is a condition where bones lose strength and break more easily. Arthritis is a group of conditions that cause pain and inflammation in joints. Osteoporosis has no symptoms until a bone breaks, while arthritis causes pain, stiffness and sometimes swelling. They are different conditions, but many people have both, and some arthritis treatments can affect bone health.

The key differences

What is affected

  • Osteoporosis affects the bones themselves, making them thinner and more fragile.
  • Arthritis affects the joints, where bones meet.

Symptoms

  • Osteoporosis is often called a "silent" condition. You will not feel bones getting weaker. The first sign is often a fracture after a minor fall, or a spinal fracture causing sudden back pain, loss of height or a stooped posture.
  • Arthritis causes joint pain, stiffness, swelling and reduced movement.

Causes

  • Osteoporosis is linked to age, menopause, low body weight, smoking, heavy drinking, family history, long-term steroid use and some medical conditions.
  • Arthritis causes depend on the type, such as joint repair problems in osteoarthritis or the immune system in rheumatoid arthritis.

Tests

  • Osteoporosis is diagnosed with a DEXA bone density scan, usually after a fracture risk assessment by your GP.
  • Arthritis is diagnosed by examination, and sometimes blood tests, X-rays or scans.

Treatment

  • Osteoporosis is treated with medicines that strengthen bones, plus calcium and vitamin D if needed, exercise and fall prevention.
  • Arthritis treatment depends on the type and includes exercise, pain relief, disease-modifying medicines and sometimes surgery.

How they are connected

  • Rheumatoid arthritis and other inflammatory conditions increase the risk of osteoporosis.
  • Steroid tablets taken for three months or more weaken bones.
  • Reduced activity because of joint pain weakens bones and muscles.
  • Falls are more common in people with painful, stiff joints, and falls are what usually lead to fractures.
  • Both conditions become more common with age, so many older people have both.

Interestingly, people with osteoarthritis do not seem to have lower bone density, but their fall risk can still be higher.

Who should have their bone health checked?

NICE (CG146) recommends fracture risk assessment for:

  • all women aged 65 and over and men aged 75 and over
  • younger people with risk factors such as a previous fragility fracture, long-term steroid use, rheumatoid arthritis, low body weight, smoking or heavy drinking, a family history of hip fracture, or early menopause

If you have arthritis and any of these, ask your GP about an assessment.

Protecting your bones and joints together

  • exercise: weight-bearing activity such as walking, plus strength exercise, helps bones and joints. Balance exercises reduce falls.
  • eat well: include calcium-rich foods such as dairy, fortified plant milks, tinned fish with bones and green leafy vegetables
  • vitamin D: follow NHS advice on vitamin D, especially in autumn and winter
  • stop smoking and limit alcohol
  • prevent falls: keep your home well lit and clutter-free, wear supportive shoes and have your eyesight checked
  • review medicines: ask about bone protection if you take steroids long term

Exercise if you have osteoporosis

Exercise is safe and helpful for most people with osteoporosis. If you have had spinal fractures, avoid sudden, forceful forward bending or twisting, and ask a physiotherapist for guidance. Strength and balance programmes are often available locally.

Common misunderstandings

  • Osteoporosis is not painful in itself. Pain comes from fractures.
  • Arthritis does not turn into osteoporosis, or the other way round.
  • Men can get osteoporosis too.
  • It is never too late to start protecting your bones.

When to see your GP

See your GP if you have joint pain or stiffness that lasts more than a few weeks, if you have broken a bone after a minor fall, or if you have lost height or developed a curved upper back. You can also ask for a fracture risk assessment if you have risk factors.

When to get urgent help

Call 999 or go to A&E if you have:

  • a joint that suddenly becomes hot, red, swollen and very painful, especially if you feel feverish or unwell (this can be a joint infection)
  • chest pain, sudden breathlessness, or signs of a stroke such as face drooping, arm weakness or slurred speech

Contact NHS 111 or your GP the same day if symptoms are getting worse quickly, you cannot put weight on a leg, or you are worried and not sure where to go. If you are under a rheumatology team, use their advice line for flares and medicine questions.
